body.heading: The phone with no battery
paragraphs: This telephone has no wires to plug in, no battery and no signal — yet it can carry a whisper across a whole garden, clearer than shouting. It worked for children a hundred years ago and it works today, because it runs on pure physics: vibrations.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The cups — two paper cups: one is the mouthpiece, one is the earpiece, and both jobs swap every turn. The string — a long piece of cotton string or wool, the road the sound travels on. The knots — the string is tied through each cup's base so the cup and string move as one. The secret ingredient — TENSION: the string must be pulled tight, or the phone goes dead.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: Two paper cups, a long piece of string or wool (5–10 metres), a sharp pencil or skewer for the holes (grown-up's job), and two people. Optional: paper clips to tie the string to, which makes a stronger join.

paragraphs: Step 1 — A grown-up pokes one small hole in the centre of each cup's base. Thread the string through and tie a big knot (or tie to a paper clip) inside each cup so it cannot pull out.
Step 2 — Walk apart until the string is pulled TIGHT and straight, not touching anything — no trees, fences or fingers along its length. A string that sags or touches things is a broken phone.

Step 3 — Talk and listen. One person puts a cup over their ear; the other speaks right into their cup, normal voice, no shouting. The voice arrives — small, tinny and astonishingly clear. Swap roles and reply.

Step 4 — Test the science. Let the string go slack: the phone dies. Pinch the string mid-call: silence. Let a friend hold the string against a fence post: the call fades. Each test proves the same law — the sound is travelling THROUGH the string.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: Your voice is moving air — vibrations. Speaking into the cup makes its base vibrate, and because the knot ties the base to the string, the vibrations climb onto the string and race along it as tiny squeezes and stretches. At the far end they shake the second cup's base, which shakes the air into your partner's ear: sound again. Sound travels far better through tight solids than through open air — your whisper would scatter in the wind, but the string keeps every vibration in line. That is why the string must be taut: a slack string swallows the vibrations before they arrive.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Why does pinching the string in the middle silence the phone?
2. Would a wire work better than wool? A ribbon? Predict which road carries sound best, then test with a grown-up.

takeaway: A taut string carries sound vibrations from cup to cup far better than open air — slacken or pinch the string and the vibrations die before they arrive.
materials: Sharp pencil or skewer for holes (grown-up only)
supervision: A grown-up makes the cup holes and supervises; the string route is chosen together, safely away from walkways.
safetyNotes: STRING SAFETY: the telephone string is never looped around necks, wrists or any body part, never strung across doors, stairs or paths where someone could walk into it, and is rolled up and put away the moment the game ends.
Hole-poking is a grown-up's job with the cup on a table, pointing away from hands.
Calls happen at garden distance with everyone in sight — children stay where their grown-up can see them, however far the string reaches.
screenFreeExtension: Secret message relay: one caller whispers a three-word message; the listener must repeat it exactly to win the round. Best of five — then swap in a longer string and try again.
